name: Colin Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign. Your words are confidential, so tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior developer at a tech company that makes household energy-bill software. I fix small calculation bugs and test whether meter readings show on the right bill, then a senior developer checks my work. I have a two-year college diploma and I'm still learning the tricky parts. I use AI tools every day to try out explanations, but a bill has to match the meter, not the explanation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do work and money fit around your family?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner does catering for events, so the income jumps with bookings. Our children are seven and thirteen, and we have a mortgage. My pay is ordinary for a developer, we've saved about two months of expenses, and there are a few similar software jobs nearby. I like trying a new tool early, but I keep the mortgage amount written above my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team that the code helper can check a simple meter calculation, but we still need to compare it with an actual bill. A little time saved is good. I wouldn't pretend an energy account has no human story behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already watching the mortgage because catering bookings are uneven. Two months saved gives us some breathing room, but a quiet event season can use it. If AI only trims routine work, I think my job stays, yet the household still feels exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing meter-bill errors and checking the helper's results against real readings. Starting this month, we'd put a set amount from every catering payment into our emergency account whenever the mortgage and food are covered. In the first year I'd keep the same developer hours and ask the billing team for a list of recurring errors to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. The software change doesn't frighten me, but the next catering calendar might. A good event week can make us feel richer than we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first expense you cut in a slow catering month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We skip takeout meals before touching the children's school needs. I would tell my partner the number at the start of the month, not after the account is low. We have done that twice this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What meter error would you bring to the helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One bill counted the same reading twice after a customer moved house. I'd put that case in the test set and ask a senior developer to check the answer. A neat paragraph can't make the extra charge right.

say: I'd use the **code helper** on simple meter checks while people verify actual bills.
I'd welcome **small time savings** without changing how we sign off charges.
think: I worry more about **uneven catering income** and the mortgage than modest AI.
Our **two-month buffer** could shrink during a quiet event season even if my job holds.
do: Keep **fixing meter errors** and checking each result against actual readings.
Transfer a **set amount** from catering payments to emergency savings only after mortgage and food are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about variable household income, though the software work remains steady.
S0.quote: A neat paragraph can't make the extra charge right.
fieldNote: He uses AI daily but grounds the answer in a **real meter reading**.
A two-month buffer does not remove **catering-season uncertainty** from the mortgage.
New savings depend on **cash after essentials**, not on assuming every event pays.

steps.text: Keep checking meter-bill fixes against actual customer readings
Transfer a set amount from catering payments only after mortgage and food are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AI can write routine bill code and answer common customer questions, so we should test wrong-charge cases before chasing speed. I would volunteer to run the trial. I'd ask management how many junior shifts it expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could be cut, because my work is mostly the small fixes that AI learns first. Using it every day may make me useful for a trial, but it doesn't make a junior wage hard to replace. My partner's event work can't promise a fixed amount each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'd build a new test list of move-house and double-charge cases with a senior developer and learn the firm's AI billing tool against it during paid time. I'd ask for the staffing forecast in writing. If my hours fall in the first year, we'd stop takeout entirely and I'd apply for local energy-software support jobs while keeping any paid hours I still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I enjoy testing something new, and I expect the company may cut my paid work after the trial. Those two thoughts sit together every time I open a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a customer with a double charge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a person will compare the meter dates and reverse the wrong line if needed. I wouldn't send them back to an automated answer that already failed. A small bill error can eat a week's food money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the trial helped rather than just sped things up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count wrong charges that reach customers, not only how many lines of code appear. If even one move-house bill is doubled, the senior developer and I would trace it before release. I would show management that number.

say: I'd test **wrong-charge cases** before using AI to speed billing code and customer replies.
I'd ask for a **junior-hours forecast** before agreeing the trial makes staffing safe.
think: I expect my **paid junior hours** could shrink once AI takes small fixes.
My daily AI use may help the trial but won't secure a **replaceable wage**.
do: Learn the **new AI billing tool** on a paid-time test of move-house errors next week.
Request a **written hours forecast** and track wrong charges reaching customers.
Stop **takeout meals** and apply for local energy-support jobs if developer hours fall.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely paid-hour cuts despite interest in the new tool.
S1.quote: A small bill error can eat a week's food money.
fieldNote: His daily AI habit does not erase the **junior wage risk** from routine automation.
He measures a trial by **wrong customer charges**, not only development speed.
Takeout cuts and local applications depend on **reduced hours**.

steps.text: Learn the new AI billing tool on paid time using move-house billing tests
Stop household takeout meals if paid developer hours fall
Apply for local energy-software support jobs if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company that thinking AI by 2028 could do the billing code and complaints before robots reach catering kitchens around 2031. I'd ask for clear layoff dates and a human way to appeal a wrong charge. My partner's cooking work may last longer than my screen work, but that doesn't fix our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer wage could go and catering alone wouldn't reliably pay for the house. Two months saved is a short bridge, especially with two children. I can try many tools, but none can make a customer pay us a wage for a job that no longer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow we'd cancel the planned summer trip and list the mortgage against a low catering month. I'd apply now to paid utility customer-support and meter-office openings, and ask my manager for a reference. In the first year after 2028, if development ends, I'd accept a paid utility role only if one is offered and ask the lender about payment options before missing the mortgage; I would pay for any required course only if food and two months of essentials remain covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have applications to make, but I expect a large wage loss very soon. A fast learner still needs a pay cheque before the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner what one slow catering month pays and compare it with the mortgage. We could cancel the trip together now, before a layoff. I don't want the children to hear our budget from a missed payment letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would utility support also be automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably some of it. I'd ask what paid work is actually left and take an offer if it helps us through the first year. I wouldn't call it a permanent shelter from AGI.

say: I'd seek **layoff dates** as 2028 thinking AI reaches code and complaints.
I'd insist on a **human bill appeal** while noting catering robots arrive later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could disappear before our two-month buffer grows.
My partner's **seasonal catering pay** cannot reliably carry the mortgage and children alone.
do: Cancel the **summer trip** and compare the mortgage with a slow catering month tomorrow.
Apply for **paid utility openings** now; accept an offered role if development ends.
Ask the **lender before missed payment** if laid off; buy required training only with food and two months protected.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected large wage loss and a short household buffer.
S2.quote: A fast learner still needs a pay cheque before the mortgage date.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 thinking AI** reaching his screen job before robots affect catering around 2031.
New utility applications start **now**, while acceptance of a paid role depends on developer work ending.
The trip is a **spending cut**; lender help and required training remain conditional.

steps.text: Cancel the planned family summer trip before 2028
Apply for paid utility jobs now; accept an offer if development ends
Take required utility course only if food and two months of essentials remain covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team five years is time to learn the utility's work, not just newer coding tools. Thinking AI in 2031 could still do the code before robots reach catering kitchens around 2034. I'd ask for a yearly headcount plan and paid visits to the meter office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn how to settle a disputed reading and build a bigger cash buffer. I don't know whether the utility will pay people for that in 2031, so I won't quit a real wage for a hoped-for desk. Our catering income will still vary meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd enroll in the utility's meter-record course if my employer covers the fee and paid time; otherwise I'd take an affordable evening course only if actual paid vacancies require it and our two-month buffer stays intact. We'd transfer a fixed amount from each developer pay cheque toward four months of essentials. In the first year after 2031, if coding hours fall and a paid meter-office vacancy exists, I'd apply while keeping any paid development hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Five years lets me collect evidence and learn with a wage coming in. I still plan household spending around the quiet catering months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the meter office teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow a reading that a family disputes from the photo to the corrected bill. My code tests tell me whether the arithmetic runs; they don't tell me whether the reading belongs to that house. I'd want to handle one case with a supervisor beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no paid meter-office jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer hours I have and look at the other nearby software firms. I wouldn't pay for a course just because the certificate looks useful. The fee has to point to a real job and leave our two months untouched.

I'd remind colleagues that **2034 robots** may later reach catering kitchens.

I won't leave a **real wage** for a meter-office role that may not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that ten years can be used to learn why a bill is wrong, not only how to make a screen faster. I'd ask the company to give juniors paid time with utility staff. Thinking AI in 2036 still reaches code before physical robots reach catering kitchens around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be a better developer or have paid utility experience by then. Our two-month buffer and seasonal catering income still make today a bit tense, even with a decade to prepare. I wouldn't promise the children a bigger house from a future job that isn't offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the developer job and try for one paid meter-office day each month if the company agrees. We'd save a small amount after mortgage and food on every developer payday and review it after the catering season. I'd complete a formal utility-billing course only if an employer pays or required paid vacancies justify a fee beyond two months of essentials. In the first year after 2036, if coding hours fall and a paid utility opening exists, I'd apply before giving notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not from the 2036 date alone. The next quiet catering season still matters to the mortgage. Ten years gives me time to learn, yet it doesn't pay next month's bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to see in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my children to see us save steadily in good event months and pull back in slow ones without panic. I don't want them to learn that every new tool is a threat. I also won't tell them a certificate guarantees a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for a billing course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd ask the employer about paid study first, then check paid vacancies and our savings above two months. A course fee must not eat the mortgage reserve. I can keep learning on real cases while I have this job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Coding could stop paying before I learn the utility's other work, and catering is too seasonal to cover our mortgage alone. Written notice, paid meter-office training, real utility vacancies and clear lender options would help us move without guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens when a wrong meter reading becomes a family argument over a bill. A customer can understand every word on a screen and still need someone to correct the number. I want that person paid and reachable.

headlineQuote: A customer can understand every word on a screen and still need someone to correct the number.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, fixing household energy-bill software while learning.
He has **typical pay**, a catering partner with seasonal bookings, two school-age children, a mortgage and two months saved.
He uses AI **daily**, yet judges its answers against actual meter readings.
Existing catering swings make **AI Plateau anxious**; faster automation threatens his junior wage and alarms him.
Longer timelines allow **meter-office training**, but every course and job move must protect the mortgage and require paid openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his coding wage while catering pay cannot reliably carry the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid meter-office training, real utility vacancies and clear lender options would help.
